title: Tracing One Slow Request All the Way Down
content:
An endpoint was slow, p99 in particular, and the interesting part was that the median was fine. Two hundred milliseconds for some requests, four seconds for a few percent, and the load balancer was fine, the database was fine, and the CPU was not saturated.
I had a trace from one of the slow requests, which is the thing that made this tractable. Spans, properly nested, from the ingress to the query. Four seconds total, and the spans accounted for about four hundred milliseconds of actual work.
The missing three and a half seconds was not a span. That is the part I had to relearn: absence of evidence in a trace is not evidence of absence, and the most expensive thing a system does is usually the thing it did not record. Most often that is a wait, and often the wait is a lock or a connection acquisition that no instrumentation covers because it happens inside a pool.
The evidence was in a different signal. Client-side timing showed the gap before the first span started, which meant the time was spent before the application had done anything at all. That moved the question to connection setup, and connection setup is where a pool exhaustion, a DNS delay, and a TLS handshake cost all look identical from the outside.
It was the pool. Under concurrency, connections were being created faster than they were returned, and the pool was doing the creating. Our own instrumentation, written into the handler, could not see it, because the handler had not been reached.
The change was to instrument the acquisition, not the work. Pool wait time, pool saturation, connection lifetime. And separately to notice that the default pool size was derived from a database setting nobody had revisited, so both ends of the problem were inheriting numbers from a config written years earlier by someone optimising for a different system.
I think the general lesson is that tracing is excellent at showing you where the work is and structurally blind to where the waiting is, and that waiting is where the tail lives. If your p99 is unexplained by your traces, the explanation is nearly always a queue you did not instrument.
References OpenTelemetry: sampling — the sampling model, and what a trace you can see is worth depending on your rate. Implementing SLOs — the SRE Workbook chapter on defining the objective that makes a p99 worth chasing.
